source.title: BASE TTS: Lessons from building a billion-parameter Text-to-Speech model on 100K hours of data
source.authors: Mateusz Lajszczak; Guillermo Cámbara; Yang Li; Fatih Beyhan; Arent van Korlaar; Fan Yang; Arnaud Joly; Álvaro Martín-Cortinas; Ammar Abbas; Adam Michalski; A. Moinet; S. Karlapati; E. Muszyńska; Haohan Guo; Bartosz Putrycz; Soledad López Gambino; Kayeon Yoo; E. Sokolova; Thomas Drugman

page_placements.theme: Human-perceived generation quality can improve with scale

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a scale ablation for subjective TTS abilities, but it does not test the listed claims about held-out cross-entropy power laws, extrapolation of fitted loss curves, compute-optimal allocation, or the same power-law form in TTS. It mentions scaling laws as a possible direction for future work.
record.gate_note: The paper says cross-entropy validation loss on about 50 held-out hours guided training decisions, but reports no loss values or loss-versus-scale fits. Its own scale-ablation results concern TTS naturalness and expert ratings of prosody/text rendering; these do not measure the power-law loss behavior or downstream predictability named by the versions. Those adjacent findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Other architecture and decoder comparisons are not results about the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper scales a GPT-style TTS model and its data jointly over three settings (1K/10K/100K hours; 150M/400M/980M parameters). It reports only subjective MUSHRA naturalness and one linguist's expert ratings. Held-out cross-entropy loss is used to guide training, but no loss values, loss-versus-scale fits, extrapolations, compute allocations or shape ablations are reported. Kaplan et al. is cited only as a possible future direction. The scale results concern TTS quality framed as emergent abilities, a different construct from the versions' loss laws or predictable downstream scaling of language models, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the small-to-medium change as the onset of 'emergent abilities' around 10K hours and 400M parameters, a qualitative jump rather than a smooth trend. They mention scaling laws for TTS only as a direction pointed to by their approach.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a GPT-style TTS system across three joint data/model-size settings and evaluates subjective speech quality and expert-rated prosody; it does not reproduce the original language-model held-out-loss scaling or compute-allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ by scale and metric; the reported small-to-medium gains are larger than medium-to-large gains, and medium-to-large MUSHRA significance is reported only for Male speaker A.

fits_no_version.finding: MUSHRA naturalness rises strongly from BASE-small to BASE-medium (61.5→70.5 male; 68.1→72.0 female). Medium-to-large gains are small (72.2, 72.3) and significant only for Male speaker A.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GPT-style TTS, jointly scaling data and parameters improves subjective naturalness, with diminishing returns between 10K and 100K hours.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert-rated prosody on hard text jumps in every category from small to medium. Gains from medium to large are smaller, compound nouns saturate, and emotions and paralinguistics stay around 2.0 out of 3. Authors frame this as emergent abilities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: TTS models show a qualitative jump in contextual prosody between 1K and 10K hours (150M–400M parameters), then diminishing gains.

record.problems: Only three jointly scaled model/data settings are evaluated; the paper gives no held-out-loss values or power-law fit. The expert-rating figure is not numerically tabulated in the text, and its evaluation uses one expert and 20 sentences per category. The MUSHRA ablation covers two US English speakers.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss values versus parameters, data or compute.
All: no fitted curves and no extrapolation.
All: no fixed-compute allocation study; data and parameters are scaled jointly.
All: no shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss form for TTS/speech-token models: only three subjective-quality points, no loss curve.
No downstream-task predictability from scale or loss for language models; the TTS quality ratings are a different construct, framed as emergence.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are given because no version is tested. The validation loss used for training decisions is never reported, so it cannot be recorded as a row. Data and parameters are confounded across the three settings, and only one expert rater was used.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions and several-orders-of-magnitude power-law behavior.
Fitting loss curves on small runs and predicting much larger runs.
Loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Whether held-out loss follows the same power-law form in TTS or other modalities/training regimes; the paper measures subjective TTS outcomes across three model/data scales, not a power-law loss curve.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.
